Information for any future Gulches regarding US tax investment from New Zealand and Australia. A lot of boring shit, but worth some thought.

Figures can be scaled up and down accordingly without too much difference until you start getting into the under $10k or over $200k ranges.

There is a lot of land available in the areas currently being looked at with long term financing at 6% real interest, sometimes lower I've seen.

For a foreigner it makes a fair bit of sense to finance and set aside the money in your own national bank, if it is paying a higher rate in corporate bond returns that are pretty much guaranteed (it would take an entire collapse of the monetary system, in which case doesn't matter anyway) and a running yield of around ~11% currently.

E.g the land costs $50k, financed for 10 years is ~$6,000 per year. The return assuming no re-investment and hold to maturity would be $5,500. This is assuming that interest rates don't fall to 0 or negative for the post-maturity period, even if they do the money is already there to be converted to a different asset class i.e. the property.

Off a 0$ deposit (wouldn't do anyway as a matter of principle) it is possible to attain e.g a $50k property, with at least the first 5 years guaranteed at maximum $500 in finance costs per year. As much as I dislike debt, this isn't true debt, there are times when using the system to your advantage like this is worthwhile.

After currency conversion fees, means that there is no large price to the finance of a property that can be expanded upon at ease and has the requirements a Gulch needs, and at any time if they decide to try to take possession or some shit the mortgage contract can be paid out in full within a couple of business days.

The other advantage for foreigners, depending on country, is that we can sometimes claim an offset against property tax paid to state of Texas against our domestic income, which for a $50k assessed value is ~$1000 or so from what I understand.

So, even if exchange rates between countries dropped 10% for the borrower's side, they would still be only slightly in the red.

These figures don't include initial settlement costs, which don't seem to be much.

From this point in a Gulch, the foreign borrower should create a series of options for the property, as no Goat should be expected to create value on land they don't own.

I can think of the following:

  • Outright purchase. Self-explanatory.

  • Lease-to-own at CPI + share of minor interest costs i.e. the $500 or so per year divided per borrower. (Anyone that can work from their computer could be an option for.)

  • Homesteading lease-to own - basically share of interest costs as above, plus use of land to payout borrower/other owners. (Agriculturalists/hunters/primary industries)

  • Labour lease-to-own - same as above but with labour (e.g. electricians, carpenters, plumbers, mechanics). This would have to be recorded by the group involved as it isn't quite as clear cut as the other options, aside from materials and may require an additional payment if there isn't the work available.

Aside from outright purchase, abandonment clauses would have to be included to stop people from getting free rent for a long period of time in promise for labour or return from the land.

I'm unsure of the situation with joint borrowing in the US, it is quite difficult here, mainly due to our ridiculously high income to housing price ratio. It seems a lot laxer over there though, so this could increase available capital also.

Let me know your thoughts, if I've missed any major points on tax or ownership to be addressed or other ideas for purchase I've missed as this is just a late night draft so far.
